fixes.explanation: Hospitality to strangers, yes. The writer says that by doing it “…some people have entertained angels without knowing it.” That's why I'd wipe down every counter in my bakery for any stranger who walks in. Nobody gets the crumby table, friend.

No guard in this verse, friend. The writer says to remember those in prison “…as if you were bound with them…” The comparison is being bound with them, not watching the door. He says the same about those who are mistreated, as if you were suffering with them.

This is the reason the writer gives. He says to be content with what you have, for God has said, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” The cookie jar may run low, friend, but that promise doesn't. Having God with you is a lot of treasure.

The writer doesn't give that reason. He says to be content with what you have, for God has said, “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” So contentment rests on God staying with you. A fat wallet isn't part of the argument.

A reward coming soon isn't mentioned in this verse. The writer's reason is what God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” Notice the reason isn't about what you hold in your hands. It's about who stays with you.

True. Right after the promise, the writer says we say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?” The confidence comes from God staying close. And that question at the end makes me stand up a little taller.

It's true, friend. Right after “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.” the writer says we say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?” Notice the word so. The promise comes first, and the confidence follows from it.

Imitate is it. The writer says to remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you, consider the outcome of their way of life, and “…imitate their faith.” Notice what he points to: their faith. That's the part to copy, friend.
Dreams aren't in this verse. The writer says, “Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings…” So the danger he names is teachings, and he calls them strange. Dream all you like, friend.

Riches aren't named in this verse. The writer says it's good for the heart to be strengthened “…by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them.” Grace is the strength-giver here. Not one chocolate chip of riches in that line.
Tablets aren't in this passage at all. The writer says, “Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.” That's what he says we carry. Not tablets, friend.

Earning trust isn't what the writer says. He says leaders “…watch over your souls as those who must give an account.” The weight on them is answering for that watching. Trust isn't the word he uses, friend.

Judgments aren't the word. The writer says, “…equip you with every good thing to do His will.” So he asks God to equip them for doing His will. Then he adds, “And may He accomplish in us what is pleasing in His sight through Jesus Christ…”

The writer says the opposite. He says, “I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly.” So he calls his letter brief, not long. That's why True isn't the pick, friend.

Released, yes. The writer says, “Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released.” Then he adds that if Timothy arrives soon, he will come with him to see them. So the news about Timothy comes with a possible visit.
True. The writer says, “If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you.” The plan hangs on that if, friend: Timothy has to arrive soon. I think it's a warm way to end a letter.
